title: The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David
summary: Jacob's lion of Judah and Isaiah's shoot from Jesse become the conquering Messiah, who appears in Revelation as a slain Lamb.

stops.note: Jacob calls Judah a lion's cub and promises that the sceptre will not depart from Judah until the one comes to whom the obedience of the peoples belongs.
A shoot will come out from the stump of Jesse and a branch grow from his roots, a new David from a cut-down royal line.
On that day the root of Jesse will stand as a signal for the peoples, and the nations will seek him.
The LORD will raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign as king and do justice in the land.
Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 from the Greek version to show that the root of Jesse rises to rule the Gentiles, who hope in him.
An elder tells weeping John that the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered and can open the scroll.
Jesus names himself the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star, in the book's closing words.

meaning: The lion stands for the royal strength promised to Judah, and the root or shoot stands for a Davidic king who would rise again after the dynasty seemed finished. Together they name the expected Messiah who would rule Israel and draw the nations. Revelation keeps both titles but redefines the victory: the Lion who has conquered is seen as a Lamb standing as though slain, so the Messiah wins by sacrificial death.
culture: The lion was a common royal symbol in the Ancient Near East, from Assyrian royal lion hunts to the lion-lined processional way of Babylon. Second Temple Jews read Genesis 49:10 messianically: a Qumran commentary on Genesis (4Q252) says the sceptre waits for the coming of the Messiah of righteousness, the Branch of David, and in 4 Ezra 11-12 a lion roaring from the forest is the Messiah who rebukes the eagle, usually taken as Rome. In the Roman world emperors claimed the right to rule the peoples, so a Jewish king of the nations was a rival claim.
compare: Revelation 5:5-6 sets what John hears beside what he sees: he is told of a Lion and turns to see a Lamb, which reinterprets the militant hope rather than discarding it. Isaiah's root is a shoot growing from Jesse, but Revelation 22:16 calls Jesus both root and descendant of David, which many read as claiming he is both source and offspring of the line. Paul uses Isaiah 11:10 for the Gentile mission, while Revelation uses it within a heavenly enthronement scene.
views: All four schools identify the Lion and Root with Christ. Preterists, idealists and amillennial readers usually see Revelation 5 as Christ's enthronement after his resurrection and ascension, while many futurists place the scene in heaven before a future tribulation, and premillennial readers expect the Davidic reign to be fully realised on earth in the millennium.

title: The bright morning star
summary: The star out of Jacob and the dawn of salvation become a title of Jesus and a promise to those who conquer.

stops.note: Balaam sees a star coming out of Jacob and a sceptre rising out of Israel to crush Moab.
The king of Babylon is mocked as the Day Star, son of Dawn, fallen from heaven after trying to raise his throne above the stars of God.
For those who fear the LORD's name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings.
Zechariah sings that the dawn from on high will break upon us, giving light to those who sit in darkness.
The prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.
To the one who conquers in Thyatira Christ promises to give the morning star, alongside authority over the nations.
Jesus calls himself the bright morning star, linking the title directly to his Davidic descent.

meaning: The morning star, the planet Venus as seen before sunrise, announces that night is ending and day is near. In Numbers the star is a coming ruler from Israel, and the prophets and Gospels speak of a dawning of salvation. Revelation applies the title to Jesus as the Davidic king whose rising signals the new day, and promises that his faithful people will share in it.
culture: Venus as morning and evening star was linked with gods across the ancient world, such as Ishtar in Mesopotamia and Phosphoros or Lucifer, the light-bringer, in Greek and Latin. The Damascus Document (CD 7.18-21) and the Qumran Testimonia (4Q175) read the star of Numbers 24:17 as a messianic figure, and in AD 132 Simon ben Kosiba was hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star', on the strength of this verse. Roman imperial propaganda also used stars and dawn imagery for the emperor's divine favour and the deified Caesars.
compare: Isaiah 14:12 uses the image for a proud king who falls, while Revelation 22:16 gives it to Jesus who rises, so the same picture can describe a usurper or the true king. Numbers' star is a conqueror over Moab; Revelation joins the star to the shepherding rule of Psalm 2 in 2:26-28. Second Peter places the rising of the morning star in believers' hearts, while Revelation presents the star as a gift that is ultimately Christ himself.
views: Most interpreters of every school take the promised morning star as Christ himself, or a share in his royal glory, given to the faithful. Futurist and historicist readers tend to stress its fulfilment at his return, preterists and idealists the present reign of the risen Christ, and Spiritual Understanding readers the dawning of Christ within the believer, as in 2 Peter 1:19.

title: Faithful witness, firstborn of the dead, ruler of the kings of the earth
summary: Three titles from the royal Psalm 89 present Jesus as the true witness, the first to rise, and the king over all kings.

stops.note: God promises to make David his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.
David's throne will be established for ever like the moon, a faithful witness in the skies.
God made David a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander for the peoples.
Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
Christ is the head of the body, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might be pre-eminent in everything.
John greets the churches from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.
To Laodicea Christ speaks as the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God's creation.

meaning: Psalm 89 gathers the promises to David: a firstborn son who stands above all kings and a throne as lasting as the moon, the faithful witness in the sky. Revelation applies all three ideas to Jesus, who bore true witness to God even to death, was the first to rise to the life of the age to come, and now holds authority over earthly rulers. The titles set the pattern for his followers, who are also called to be faithful witnesses, like Antipas in Revelation 2:13.
culture: In the Ancient Near East the king was often called the son or firstborn of a god, and Psalm 89 uses that language for David. In Greek 'witness' is martys, and by the second century the word was already coming to mean a martyr, one who testifies by dying. In Roman Asia the emperor was honoured as ruler of the world and client kings depended on him, so calling a crucified Jew the ruler of the kings of the earth was a political as well as a religious claim. Laodicea lay close to Colossae, and Colossians 4:16 mentions a letter to the Laodiceans, so the echo of 'firstborn' and 'beginning' in 3:14 may reflect language already known there.
compare: Psalm 89 is a lament that the Davidic promise seems broken, and Revelation answers it with a king whose throne is secure because he has passed through death. The psalm's faithful witness is the moon; in Revelation it is a person whose testimony cost his life. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits and firstborn of the dead to ground the coming resurrection of believers, and Revelation uses the title as a source of courage for those facing death.
views: The titles are not disputed between the schools, but the scope of 'ruler of the kings of the earth' is: preterists, postmillennialists and amillennial idealists stress Christ's present reign since the resurrection, while futurists and historic premillennialists often see it as rightful now but publicly enforced only at his return.

title: A kingdom of priests
summary: Israel's calling at Sinai to be a priestly kingdom passes to the redeemed of every nation, who reign with Christ.

stops.note: At Sinai God tells Israel that if they keep his covenant they will be to him a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
The restored people will be called priests of the LORD and ministers of God, and will enjoy the wealth of the nations.
The holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it for ever.
The kingdom and dominion under the whole heaven are given to the people of the holy ones of the Most High.
Believers are built as living stones into a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices.
Peter applies Exodus 19:6 to the churches: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation.
Christ, who freed us by his blood, has made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father.
The new song says the Lamb made people from every tribe and nation a kingdom and priests, and they shall reign on the earth.
Those who share in the first resurrection will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with him a thousand years.

meaning: To be a kingdom of priests is to belong wholly to God, to have access to him, and to stand between God and the nations as his representatives. Israel received this calling at Sinai, and the prophets looked for its renewal, while Daniel adds that the saints will share the kingdom itself. Revelation says the Lamb's death has created this priestly, ruling people out of every nation, and that they will reign.
culture: Ancient Near Eastern kings often acted as chief priests, so joining royalty and priesthood was familiar, but Exodus extends it to a whole people. The Greek translation renders Exodus 19:6 as 'a royal priesthood' (basileion hierateuma), the form 1 Peter quotes, and Jubilees 16:18 and 33:20 echo the phrase for Israel; the Qumran community saw itself as a priestly holy house. In Roman Asia the high priests of the imperial cult were drawn from wealthy elites, while Revelation gives priesthood to ordinary believers, including the poor and the slave.
compare: Exodus makes the calling conditional on keeping the covenant; Revelation grounds it in what Christ has already done through his blood. Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 follow the Hebrew 'a kingdom, priests' rather than the Greek 'royal priesthood' used by Peter. Daniel's saints receive the kingdom after the beasts are judged, and Revelation 5:10 and 20:6 likewise speak of reigning, which makes timing a key question.
views: Amillennial idealists and many preterists hold that believers already reign as priests now, with Revelation 20:6 describing the present reign of believers or of departed saints with Christ; postmillennialists stress the gospel's growing influence. Premillennial futurists and historic premillennialists take 'they shall reign on the earth' and the thousand years as a future reign after Christ's return, and some manuscripts' 'they reign' in 5:10 is part of the debate.

title: The key of David
summary: The royal steward's key over David's house becomes Christ's authority to open and shut entry into God's kingdom.

stops.note: Shebna, the steward over the royal house, is condemned for carving a grand tomb for himself and will be thrust from office.
God gives Eliakim Shebna's robe and the key of the house of David: what he opens no one will shut, and what he shuts no one will open.
Eliakim is fixed like a peg in a secure place, yet the peg will finally give way under the weight of his family.
Jesus gives Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, with authority to bind and loose.
The risen Christ says he was dead and is alive for ever, and holds the keys of Death and Hades.
To Philadelphia Christ speaks as the one who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut.
He sets before the small, faithful church an open door that no one is able to shut.

meaning: In Isaiah the key belongs to the steward who controlled access to the king and the royal household, so it means delegated authority to admit or exclude. Jesus gives keys of the kingdom to Peter, and in Revelation he holds the key himself, as the Davidic Messiah who decides who enters God's kingdom and who has power over death. For a weak church shut out by others, the promise is that the door Christ opens stays open.
culture: The office 'over the house' is known from Hebrew seal impressions and from a tomb inscription at Silwan in Jerusalem that some scholars link to Shebna. Ancient keys could be large wooden or metal objects carried on the shoulder, as Isaiah 22:22 says. In Greek religion the goddess Hecate was described as holding the keys of Hades, and some scholars, including Aune, suggest Revelation 1:18 answers such claims. Philadelphia's letter mentions 'the synagogue of Satan' (3:9), which suggests that the Christians there had been excluded from the local Jewish community.
compare: Isaiah's Eliakim is a human steward whose peg eventually gives way, but the one who holds the key in Revelation is 'the holy one, the true one', whose authority does not fail. Matthew's keys are given to an apostle for the church's ministry, while Revelation's key remains in Christ's hand. Revelation turns the language of exclusion around: those who seemed shut out are the ones before whom the door stands open.
views: Most readers see the key as Christ's messianic authority over entrance into the kingdom, and the open door as either access to the kingdom or an opportunity for mission. Some historicist and dispensational readers take Philadelphia as a picture of a later missionary era of church history, preterists tie the letter to conflict with the synagogue before AD 70, and idealists apply it to faithful churches in every age.

title: The Word of God
summary: The creating, prophetic word of God becomes the name of the rider on the white horse who judges with a sword from his mouth.

stops.note: God speaks, 'Let there be light', and there is light, so creation comes into being by his word.
By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth.
The word that goes out from God's mouth will not return empty but will accomplish what he purposes.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory.
The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, judging the thoughts of the heart.
John testifies to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, which make up the content of the book.
The rider on the white horse is clothed in a robe dipped in blood, and his name is called the Word of God.

meaning: In the Hebrew Bible God's word is his effective speech: it creates, it commands, and it accomplishes his purpose. John's Gospel identifies that word with a person who became flesh, and Hebrews describes it as a sword that judges. Revelation uses 'the word of God' for the message the martyrs hold to, and then gives the same name to Christ as he comes to judge, so the one who conquers does so by the word that comes from his mouth (19:15).
culture: Ancient Near Eastern texts sometimes speak of a god's word as a powerful force, and in Egyptian thought the god Ptah creates by speech. Greek philosophers, especially the Stoics, spoke of the Logos as the rational principle ordering the world, and the Jewish thinker Philo of Alexandria described the Logos as God's agent in creation. Aramaic Targums often use the 'Memra' or word of the LORD where the Hebrew speaks of God acting. The Wisdom of Solomon 18:15-16, a book in the Greek Old Testament, pictures God's all-powerful word leaping from the royal throne like a stern warrior with a sharp sword on the night of the Passover, a striking parallel to Revelation 19.
compare: Genesis and the Psalms present the word as creating; Revelation 19 presents it as judging, with the sword coming from the mouth rather than held in the hand. John's Gospel speaks of the Word becoming flesh in humility, while Revelation shows the same Word coming in power. The robe 'dipped in blood' recalls the treader of the winepress in Isaiah 63:1-3, where the blood is the enemies', though many interpreters think Revelation means Christ's own blood, since he is already wearing it before the battle.
views: Futurists and most historicists see Revelation 19:11-16 as the visible second coming at the end of the age. Preterists often read it as Christ's judgment on his first-century enemies or the ongoing triumph of the gospel, and idealists as the victory of Christ through his word throughout history, completed at the end; the sword from the mouth leads many in all schools to stress that he conquers by speech rather than physical weapons.

title: The two witnesses, two olive trees and two lampstands
summary: Two prophets with the powers of Moses and Elijah testify, are killed, and are raised, echoing Zechariah's olive trees and lampstand.

stops.note: Moses strikes the Nile and its waters turn to blood, the first of the plagues on Egypt.
No one may be put to death on the evidence of a single witness.
Every charge must be established on the evidence of two or three witnesses.
Elijah announces that there will be neither dew nor rain except by his word, and the drought begins.
Zechariah sees a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees beside it.
The two olive trees are explained as the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.
God promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes.
Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus on the mountain of transfiguration, talking with him.
Two witnesses, called the two olive trees and two lampstands, prophesy 1,260 days, are killed by the beast, lie unburied, and are raised and taken up to heaven.

meaning: Two witnesses make testimony legally valid, so the number points to true and sufficient witness. Their powers to shut the sky and turn water to blood recall Elijah and Moses, the prophet and the lawgiver, while Zechariah's olive trees recall the anointed king and priest of the restored community. Their story follows Jesus' own: they bear witness, are killed in the great city, and are raised and vindicated before their enemies.
culture: Zechariah's two anointed ones are usually taken as Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. Jewish tradition expected the return of Elijah, and some texts expected Enoch as well, since neither had died; the Qumran community looked for a prophet like Moses and two messiahs of Aaron and Israel. Early Christian writers such as Hippolytus and Tertullian identified the two witnesses with Enoch and Elijah. Leaving bodies unburied was a grave insult in the ancient world, and the scene of the nations gazing and exchanging gifts parodies a public festival.
compare: Zechariah has one lampstand and two olive trees; Revelation makes the witnesses both trees and lampstands, and in 1:20 lampstands are churches. Moses and Elijah each worked alone, but here the two share each other's powers. Unlike Elijah, who was taken up without dying, the witnesses die first and are then raised, following the pattern of the crucified and risen Christ.
views: Futurists usually expect two individual prophets in Jerusalem in the future tribulation, often Moses and Elijah or Enoch and Elijah. Preterists commonly see witnesses to Jerusalem before AD 70, sometimes the apostolic church, and historicists have read them as the two Testaments, the Law and the Prophets, or faithful witnesses such as the Waldensians through the 1,260 years. Idealists and many amillennial readers take them as the witnessing church as a whole, suffering and vindicated.

title: The woman clothed with the sun and her child
summary: A woman in birth pains bears the ruling son whom the dragon seeks to devour, drawing on Eden, Joseph's dream and Zion in labour.

stops.note: God sets enmity between the serpent and the woman's offspring, and tells the woman she will bear children in pain.
Joseph dreams that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him, picturing Jacob's family.
God declares the king his son and gives him the nations, to rule them with a rod of iron.
Israel is like a woman writhing in labour who gives birth only to wind, unable to bring salvation.
Before her pains came, Zion gave birth to a son, so that a nation is born in one day.
Daughter Zion must writhe like a woman in labour and go to Babylon, yet there she will be rescued.
Paul says the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.
A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars, crying out in birth pains.
She bears a male child who is to rule the nations with a rod of iron; he is caught up to God, and she flees into the wilderness for 1,260 days.

meaning: The woman gathers up the people of God as mother: Eve whose offspring will crush the serpent, Israel with its twelve tribes, and Zion in labour giving birth to salvation. Her child is the Messiah of Psalm 2, and the dragon's attempt to devour him is the ancient serpent's war against the promised offspring. After the child is taken up, the woman is protected in the wilderness, as Israel was in the exodus.
culture: Many scholars note a parallel with the Greek myth of Leto, pregnant with Apollo and pursued by the dragon Python, which was well known in Asia Minor and was used in imperial propaganda linking emperors with Apollo. Egyptian stories of Isis and Horus pursued by Set offer a similar pattern, and the goddess Roma was honoured across Asia as a queenly mother figure. In Jewish tradition the twelve stars recall the twelve tribes and the twelve signs of the zodiac, which Josephus and Philo linked with the high priest's twelve stones.
compare: Joseph's dream has eleven stars, while Revelation's woman has twelve, a complete Israel. Isaiah's Zion gives birth without pain, while Revelation's woman cries out in labour, closer to Micah. Genesis promises a coming conflict between serpent and offspring; Revelation shows it reaching its decisive point, with the child taken up and the dragon thrown down.
views: Preterists often see the faithful Jewish community bearing the Messiah and the flight as the Jerusalem church's escape before AD 70; historicists commonly read the wilderness 1,260 days as the true church's long period of obscurity under persecution. Futurists usually identify the woman as Israel, protected in a future tribulation, and idealists as the people of God in both covenants. Roman Catholic readers also see a secondary reference to Mary, and Spiritual Understanding readers may read the birth as Christ formed within the believer.

title: Michael and the war in heaven
summary: Daniel's angelic prince who stands for God's people leads the heavenly war in which the dragon, the accuser, is thrown down.

stops.note: The angel tells Daniel that the prince of Persia resisted him until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help.
No one contends on the angel's side against the princes of Persia and Greece except Michael, your prince.
At the time of the end Michael, the great prince who stands for your people, will arise in a time of unequalled trouble.
When the seventy return, Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
As the cross approaches Jesus says, 'Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be driven out.'
The archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, does not presume to condemn him but says, 'The Lord rebuke you.'
War breaks out in heaven; Michael and his angels fight the dragon, who is thrown down to the earth with his angels.
A loud voice declares that the accuser has been thrown down, and that the believers conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and their testimony.

meaning: Michael is the angelic guardian of God's people, whose name means 'Who is like God?'. In Daniel he fights the spiritual princes behind earthly empires, and in Revelation he leads the war that throws Satan out of heaven. The hymn that follows explains the battle: Satan's role as accuser is ended by the blood of the Lamb, so the heavenly victory rests on the cross.
culture: Ancient Near Eastern myth often told of a storm god defeating a sea dragon to win kingship, and Revelation 12 uses that pattern. In Second Temple Judaism Michael is named among the chief angels in 1 Enoch 20 and set over Israel, and the Qumran War Scroll (1QM 17) promises that God will raise the dominion of Michael among the angels. Early church writers say Jude 9 draws on a lost ending of the Testament or Assumption of Moses. The Satan as accuser in the heavenly court appears in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3.
compare: In Daniel Michael fights the princes of Persia and Greece, while in Revelation he fights the dragon himself. Daniel places Michael's rising at a time of great trouble before the resurrection; Revelation links his victory to the child being caught up to God, and the voice from heaven credits the believers' victory to the Lamb's blood rather than to Michael. Luke and John speak of Satan's fall in connection with Jesus' ministry and cross, which many read as the same event Revelation pictures.
views: Preterists, idealists and many amillennial readers place the war in heaven at Christ's death, resurrection and ascension, which follow the child being caught up. Futurists often place it in the middle of a future seven-year tribulation, when Satan is cast to earth for the last three and a half years. Historicists have linked it to events such as the fall of Roman paganism under Constantine, and Seventh-day Adventists identify Michael with Christ himself.

title: Locusts from the abyss
summary: The locust plague of Egypt and Joel's invading army return as demonic locusts with a king called Destroyer.

stops.note: In the eighth plague locusts cover the land of Egypt so that it is darkened and nothing green is left.
Swarm after swarm devours the land, a nation with teeth like a lion's teeth.
The locust army looks like horses, sounds like chariots, darkens sun and moon, and is the LORD's army on his day.
Amos sees God forming locusts to devour the late crop, and pleads for Jacob.
Nineveh's merchants and officials are like locusts that strip the land and fly away.
At the fifth trumpet the shaft of the abyss is opened, smoke darkens the sun, and locusts come out to torment for five months those without God's seal.
The locusts look like horses ready for battle, with human faces, women's hair and lions' teeth, and their king is the angel of the abyss, Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek.

meaning: Locusts were the most feared natural disaster in the ancient world, and the prophets used them for God's judgment and for invading armies. Revelation's locusts come from the abyss rather than the fields, do not harm vegetation but people, and torment without killing, which makes them a spiritual or demonic plague. Their king's name, Destroyer, shows what the power behind them really is.
culture: Assyrian and Mesopotamian texts compare invading armies to locust swarms, and locust plagues are recorded throughout the region. Abaddon, 'destruction', is a Hebrew poetic name for the realm of the dead (Job 26:6, 28:22, Psalm 88:11). Many scholars note that the Greek Apollyon resembles the name of the god Apollo, whose symbols in some traditions included the locust, and that emperors such as Nero and, on some accounts, Domitian were associated with Apollo, so the title may hint that the empire's patron god is really the destroyer; this is a suggestion, not a certainty. Five months roughly matches the life cycle or season of the locust, and the long hair has reminded some interpreters of Parthian horsemen.
compare: Egypt's locusts strip the land, while Revelation's are forbidden to harm grass or trees and attack only people without God's seal, echoing Israel's protection in Goshen. Joel's locusts are like horses and armies; Revelation intensifies the comparison with human faces, crowns, iron breastplates and scorpion tails. In Joel the army is the LORD's; in Revelation the locusts have their own destructive king, yet they act only within limits God sets.
views: Historicists traditionally read the fifth trumpet as the Arab or Saracen invasions of the seventh century, often counting the five months as 150 years. Futurists usually take the locusts as demonic beings released in a future tribulation, while some have suggested modern military aircraft; preterists link them to the demonic and social torment of the Jewish War before AD 70. Idealists see the self-destructive torment that evil and deception bring to those who belong to it.

title: The Euphrates and the kings from the east
summary: The river that bounded Eden, the promised land and the Roman world is dried up to open the way for kings from the east.

stops.note: The Euphrates is the fourth of the rivers flowing out of Eden.
God promises Abram's offspring the land from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates.
The LORD will wave his hand over the River and split it into seven channels, so that people can cross in sandals.
God says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers', in the verse before he names Cyrus.
A drought will come upon Babylon's waters and they will be dried up, for it is a land of idols.
The LORD will dry up Babylon's sea and make her fountain dry.
At the sixth trumpet four angels bound at the great river Euphrates are released, with a vast cavalry.
The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to prepare the way for the kings from the east.

meaning: The Euphrates marked the edge of the promised land and the gateway from which invading empires such as Assyria and Babylon came. Drying up a river recalls the exodus and the fall of Babylon, so the image signals that God is removing a barrier for his purposes. In Revelation the opened river releases hostile forces gathered for the final battle, and it is also the river of Babylon, whose fall follows in chapters 16 to 18.
culture: Herodotus (1.191) and Xenophon tell how Cyrus took Babylon by diverting the Euphrates and marching in along the riverbed, a story that fits Isaiah's and Jeremiah's drying of Babylon's waters, though the Babylonian Nabonidus Chronicle simply says the city fell without battle. In John's day the Euphrates was roughly Rome's eastern frontier, beyond which lay the Parthians, mounted archers who had defeated Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC and forced a Roman army to surrender in AD 62. 1 Enoch 56:5-7 pictures angels stirring up the Parthians and Medes against the land, and the Sibylline Oracles (4 and 5) expected Nero to return from beyond the Euphrates with eastern armies.
compare: In Isaiah the River is split so God's exiles can return; in Revelation it is dried so hostile kings can advance, which reverses the exodus pattern. Jeremiah's drying of the waters is judgment on Babylon, and Revelation keeps that link by placing the sixth bowl immediately before Babylon's fall. Revelation 9:14 and 16:12 both centre on the river, with a release of forces at the sixth trumpet and the sixth bowl.
views: Historicists traditionally read the sixth trumpet as the Turkish invasions and the drying of the Euphrates as the decline of the Ottoman Empire, opening the way for events in the east. Futurists usually expect literal armies from Asia gathering for Armageddon, while preterists point to Roman legions drawn from the Euphrates region for the war against Jerusalem, or to fears of a Parthian invasion of Rome. Idealists read the river as the boundary holding back chaos, whose removal lets evil gather for its own defeat.

title: Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified
summary: The great city where the witnesses lie is called by the names of the Bible's archetypal places of wickedness and oppression.

stops.note: The LORD rains sulphur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah and overthrows the cities of the plain.
Egypt sets taskmasters over Israel and makes their lives bitter with hard labour.
Isaiah addresses Jerusalem's rulers and people as rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah.
Jerusalem is told she is worse than her sister Sodom, whose guilt was pride, excess and neglect of the poor.
Jesus says it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for a town that rejects his messengers.
The witnesses' bodies lie in the street of the great city that is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.

meaning: Sodom stands for arrogance, violence and contempt for the vulnerable, and Egypt for oppression and slavery of God's people. The prophets already used Sodom as a name for faithless Jerusalem, so the label is a prophetic charge rather than a map reference. Revelation says the city is so called 'spiritually' or prophetically, and adds that it is the place where the Lord was crucified, so the city that kills the witnesses repeats the world's rejection of Christ.
culture: Sodom's destruction became a byword for divine judgment across Jewish literature, as in Jubilees 16 and 3 Maccabees 2:5. The Wisdom of Solomon 19:13-17 compares the Egyptians to the people of Sodom for their hostility to strangers, so joining the two names had precedent. Roman Asia's readers knew Egypt as a Roman province and grain supplier, but in Jewish memory it remained the house of bondage.
compare: Isaiah and Ezekiel call Jerusalem Sodom to shame her; Revelation adds Egypt and the crucifixion, making the charge sharper. Matthew compares towns that reject the apostles unfavourably with Sodom, and Revelation likewise places the witnesses' rejection alongside Jesus' own. In Genesis Sodom is destroyed by fire from heaven, while in Revelation 11:13 an earthquake strikes the city and the survivors give glory to God, a more hopeful outcome.
views: Preterists and many futurists take 'where their Lord was crucified' as pointing to Jerusalem, the first in its first-century state and the second in a future tribulation. Many idealists and some historicists note that 'the great city' elsewhere in Revelation is Babylon (16:19, 17:18) and read it as the world city opposed to God, including Rome, and some older historicists applied it to a particular nation such as Revolutionary France.

title: Hidden manna and the white stone
summary: The bread from heaven kept before the ark and a white stone bearing a secret new name are promised to the faithful in Pergamum.

stops.note: In the wilderness a fine, flaky substance covers the ground, and Moses tells Israel it is the bread the LORD has given them.
An omer of manna is placed in a jar before the testimony to be kept for future generations.
God rained down manna for them to eat and gave them the grain of heaven.
After the crowd recalls the manna, Jesus says that he himself is the true bread from heaven, the bread of life.
The ark of the covenant held the golden jar of manna, Aaron's staff and the tablets.
To the one who conquers in Pergamum Christ will give some of the hidden manna and a white stone with a new name that no one knows except the one who receives it.

meaning: Manna was God's daily provision in the wilderness, and the jar kept before the ark made it a lasting sign of his care. The 'hidden' manna points to heavenly food kept for the faithful, which John's Gospel identifies with Jesus himself. The white stone with a new name suggests acceptance, admission and a personal, intimate identity given by Christ, set against the idol feasts that tempted the church in Pergamum.
culture: Jewish tradition held that Jeremiah hid the ark and its contents before Jerusalem fell (2 Maccabees 2:4-8), and 2 Baruch 29:8 expects the treasury of manna to come down again from on high in the messianic age. In the Greco-Roman world small stones or tokens (tesserae) served as tickets for admission to feasts and public events, jurors voted for acquittal with white pebbles, and stones inscribed with secret names served as amulets. Pergamum was a centre of pagan cult, including the altar of Zeus, the healing shrine of Asclepius and an early temple of Augustus and Rome, where banquets in honour of gods were part of civic and guild life.
compare: The manna of Exodus was gathered openly every morning; Revelation's is hidden and given only to those who conquer. John 6 speaks of the bread of life now, while Revelation presents the manna as a future reward that answers the refusal of idol food in 2:14. The new name echoes Isaiah 62:2 and 65:15, where God's people receive a new name, but Revelation makes it known only to the one who receives it.
views: Interpreters of all schools agree that the promise is a reward for faithfulness in Pergamum, though they differ on the white stone's background, whether acquittal, admission token or amulet. Futurists often connect it with the marriage supper of the Lamb and the coming kingdom, preterists and idealists with communion with Christ now and fully at the end, and Spiritual Understanding readers with Christ as the inner bread and a new identity known only in the heart. Some historicist and dispensational readers also see Pergamum as a picture of the church in the age of Constantine.

title: Balaam, Jezebel and the Nicolaitans
summary: Two Old Testament figures who led Israel into idolatry become code names for teachers urging compromise in Pergamum and Thyatira.

stops.note: Israel, having escaped Balaam's curses, joins in the sacrificial feasts of Moab and yokes itself to the Baal of Peor.
Moses says the Midianite women acted on Balaam's advice to make Israel act faithlessly at Peor.
Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the Sidonian king, and serves Baal; 21:25 says she urged him on in evil.
Jehu tells Joram there can be no peace while the whorings and sorceries of his mother Jezebel continue.
False teachers have gone astray, following the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved gain from wrongdoing.
The intruders have abandoned themselves to Balaam's error for the sake of gain.
Christ praises the Ephesian church for hating the works of the Nicolaitans, which he also hates.
Some in Pergamum hold the teaching of Balaam, who put a stumbling block before Israel to eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality, and some hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.
Thyatira tolerates 'that woman Jezebel', a self-styled prophetess who leads believers into immorality and idol food, and who is given time to repent.

meaning: Balaam, hired by Balak of Moab (Numbers 22:5), could not curse Israel but helped draw it into idolatry, and Jezebel brought Baal worship into Israel's royal house. Revelation uses their names for teachers within the churches who encouraged eating idol food and sexual immorality, which may be literal, or the prophets' figure for unfaithfulness to God, or both. The concern is compromise from inside the church, which Christ treats as more dangerous than persecution from outside.
culture: Thyatira had many trade guilds, known from inscriptions, including wool workers, dyers, leather workers, potters and bronze smiths, and Lydia the purple seller came from there (Acts 16:14). Guild membership often involved banquets in honour of patron gods, where meat sacrificed to idols was served, so refusing could cost a person work and standing; Pergamum likewise had temples of Zeus, Asclepius and the emperor. Paul addresses similar questions about idol food in 1 Corinthians 8-10, and the Jerusalem council forbade it (Acts 15:29). Irenaeus linked the Nicolaitans to Nicolaus of Antioch (Acts 6:5), though this is uncertain, and some scholars suggest that Nicolaitan ('conquer the people') is a Greek play on a Hebrew reading of Balaam as 'consumer of the people'.
compare: Numbers presents Balaam as a foreign seer, while 2 Peter, Jude and Revelation make him a type of the false teacher motivated by gain or compromise. Jezebel in Kings is a queen who persecutes prophets; in Revelation she is a prophetess inside the church, and she is given time to repent, which the original Jezebel was not. Ephesus is praised for rejecting the Nicolaitans, while Pergamum and Thyatira are rebuked for tolerating them.
views: Preterists and idealists read these figures as real first-century teachers in Asia, and idealists also as types of compromise in every age. Some historicists and dispensational readers treat the seven churches as successive church ages, taking Pergamum as the church wedded to the state after Constantine and Thyatira as the medieval church, with Jezebel sometimes identified with corrupt Rome. Most futurists, while differing on the church ages, also read the letters as first addressed to real congregations.
